kaffir.etymology: Ar. k infidel, pagan, fr. kafara to be skeptical in religious matters; -- a name given to certain infidel races by the Mohammedans. Cf. Giaour.

kafir.etymology: Ar. k infidel, pagan, fr. kafara to be skeptical in religious matters; -- a name given to certain infidel races by the Mohammedans. Cf. Giaour.

kaiser.etymology: Gr., fr. L. Caesar. Cf. Kesar, and Czar.

kale.etymology: Scot. kale, kail, cale, colewort, Gael. cael; akin to Ir. cal, W. cawl, Armor. kaol. See Cole.

roots.meaning: A combining form usually signifying an instrument for viewing (with the eye) or observing (in any way); as in microscope, telescope, altoscope, anemoscope.

kalmia.etymology: NL. Named in honor of Peter Kalm, a Swedish botanist.

kama.etymology: Skr. kama love, the god of love.

kangaroo.etymology: Said to be the native name.

keel.etymology: AS. c to cool, fr. c cool. See Cool.

keelson.etymology: Akin to Sw. kölsvin, Dan. kjölsviin, G. kielschwein; apparently compounded of the words keel and swine; but cf. Norweg. kjölsvill, where svill is akin to E. sill, n.

keep.etymology: OE. k, AS.c to keep, regard, desire, await, take, betake; cf. AS. copenere lover, OE. copnien to desire.

keg.etymology: Earlier cag, Icel. kaggi; akin to Sw. kagge.

roots.meaning: A suffix or combining form meaning like, resembling, in the form of; as in anthropoid, asteroid, spheroid.

kelpie.etymology: Cf. Gael. cailpeach, calpach, colpach, a heifer, steer, colt, colpa a cow or horse.

kelpy.etymology: Cf. Gael. cailpeach, calpach, colpach, a heifer, steer, colt, colpa a cow or horse.

kelter.etymology: Cf. Gael. & Ir. cealt clothes, Gael. cealltair spear, castle, cause, Prov. E. kilter tool, instrument. Cf. Kilt.

keno.etymology: F. quine five winning numbers, fr. L. quini five each, quinque five. See Five.

roots.meaning: A suffix used in medical terms to denote an inflammatory disease of; as, arthritis; bronchitis, phrenitis.

kerchief.etymology: OE. coverchef, OF. cuevrechief, couvrechef, F. couvrechef, a head covering, fr. couvrir to cover + OF. chief head, F. chef. See Cover, Chief, and cf. Curfew.

kernel.etymology: OE. kernel, kirnel, curnel, AS.cyrnel, fr. corn grain. See Corn, and cf. Kern to harden.

ketch.etymology: Prob. corrupted fr. Turk. qaiq : cf. F. caiche. Cf. Caïque.

kettle.etymology: OE. ketel; cf. AS. cetel, cetil, cytel; akin to D. kjedel, G. kessel, OHG. chezzil, Icel. ketill, SW. kittel, Dan. kjedel, Goth. katils; all perh. fr. L. catillus, dim. of catinus a deep vessel, bowl; but cf. also OHG. chezzi kettle, Icel. kati small ship.

khamsin.etymology: Ar. khamsin, fr. khamsun, oblique case khamsin, fifty; -- so called because it blows for about fifty days, from April till June.

khedive.etymology: F. khédive, Pers. khediw a prince.

kid.etymology: Of Scand. origin; cf. Icel. ki, Dan. & Sw. kid; akin to OHG. kizzi, G. kitz, kitzchen, kitzlein.

kidnap.etymology: Kid a child + Prov. E. nap to seize, to grasp. Cf. Knab, Knap, Nab.

kidney.etymology: OE. kidnei, kidnere, from Icel. koi belly, womb (akin to Goth. gipus, AS. cwip womb) + OE. nere kidney; akin to D. nier, G. niere, OHG. nioro, Icel. n, Dan. nyre, Sw. njure, and probably to Gr. (Kite belly.

kieselguhr.etymology: G., fr. kiesel flint + guhr an earthy deposit or sediment in water.

kieserite.etymology: Named after Prof. Kieser, of Jena.

kilderkin.etymology: OD. kindeken, kinneken, a small barrel, orig., a little child, fr. kind child; akin to G.kind, and to E. kin.

kiln.etymology: OE.kilne, kulne, AS. cyln, cylen; akin to Icel. kylna; prob. from the same source as coal. See Coal.

kilogram.etymology: F. kilogramme; pref. kilo- (fr. Gr. chi`lioi a thousand ) + gramme. See 3d Gram.

roots.meaning: A combining form used to signify thousand in forming the names of units of measurement; as, kilogram, kilometer, kilowatt, etc.

kiloliter.etymology: F. kilolitre. See Kilogram, and Liter.

kilolitre.etymology: F. kilolitre. See Kilogram, and Liter.

kilometer.etymology: F. kilometre. See Kilogram, and Meter.

kilometre.etymology: F. kilometre. See Kilogram, and Meter.

kilt.etymology: OGael. cealt clothes, or rather perh. fr. Dan. kilte op to truss, tie up, tuck up.

kin.etymology: Of Low German origin; cf. G. -chen, LG. -- ken.

kind.etymology: AS. cynde, gecynde, natural, innate, prop. an old p. p. from the root of E. kin. See Kin kindred.

kindergarten.etymology: G., lit., children's garden; kinder (pl. of kind child, akin to E. kin kindred) + garten garden.

kindred.etymology: OE. kinrede, kynrede, kunreden (with excrescent d), fr. AS. cunn kin, race + the termination to advise, G. rathen. Cf. Hatred.

kine.etymology: For older kyen, formed like oxen, fr. AS. c, itself pl. of c cow. See Cow, and cf. Kee, Kie.

king.etymology: AS. cyng, cyning; akin to OS. kining, D. koning, OHG. kining, G. könig, Icel. konungr, Sw. koning, OHG. kuning, Dan. konge; formed with a patronymic ending, and fr. the root of E. kin; cf. Icel. konr a man of noble birth. Kin.

roots.meaning: A suffix denoting: (a) Jurisdiction or property and jurisdiction, dominion, as in kingdom earldom. (b) State, condition, or quality of being, as in wisdom, freedom.

kink.etymology: D. kink a bend or turn, or Sw. kink.

kinkajou.etymology: F. kinkajou, quincajou, from the native American name.

kipper.etymology: D. kippen to hatch, snatch, seize. Cf. Kipe.

kirk.etymology: Scot.; cf. Icel. kirkja, of Greek origin. See Church.

kirtle.etymology: OE. kirtel, curtel, AS. cyrtel; skin to Icel. kyrtill, Sw. kjortel, Dan. kiortel, kiole.

kiss.etymology: OE. kissen, cussen, AS. cyssan, fr. coss a kiss; of uncertain origin; akin to D. kus, G. kuss, Icel. koss.

kitchen.etymology: OE. kichen, kichene, kuchene, AS. cycene, L. coquina, equiv. to culina a kitchen, fr. coquinus pertaining to cooking, fr. coquere to cook. See Cook to prepare food, and cf. Cuisine.

kite.etymology: OE. kyte, AS.c; cf. W. cud, cut.

kith.etymology: OE. kith, cu, AS. cc known. Uncouth, Can, and cf. Kythe.

kitten.etymology: OE. kiton, a dim. of cat; cf. G.kitze a young cat, also a female cat, and F. chaton, dim. of chat cat, also E. kitling. See Cat.

knack.etymology: Prob. of imitative origin; cf. G. knacken to break, Dan. knage to crack, and E. knock.

knap.etymology: AS. cnæp, cnæpp, top, knob, button; cf. Icel. knappr knob, Sw. knapp, Dan. knap button, W., Gael., & Ir. cnap knob, button, and E. knop.

knapsack.etymology: D. knapzak; knappen to eat + zak a bag. See Knap, v. t., and Sack.

knave.etymology: OE., boy, servant, knave, AS. cnafa boy, youth; cf. AS. cnapa boy, youth, D. kna, G. knabe boy, knappe esquire, Icel. knapi, Sw. knape esquire, knäfvel knave.

knawel.etymology: Akin to G. knauelk, knäuel,prop., a ball of thread, coil. Cf. Clew.

knead.etymology: OE. kneden, As. cnedan; akin to D. kneden, G. kneten, Sw. kn, Icel. kno; cf. OSlav.gnesti.

knee.etymology: OE. kne, cneo, As. cneó, cneów; akin to OS. knio, kneo, OFries. kni, G. & D. knie, OHG. chniu, chneo, Icel. kn, Sw. knä,Dan. knæ, Goth. kniu, L.genu, Gr. janu, Cf. Genuflection.

kneel.etymology: OE. knelen, cneolien; akin to D. knielen, Dan. knæle. See Knee.

knell.etymology: OE. knel, cnul, AS. cnyll, fr. cnyllan to sound a bell; cf. D. & G. knallen to clap, crack, G. & Sw. knall a clap, crack, loud sound, Dan. knalde to clap, crack. Cf. Knoll, n. & v.

knife.etymology: OE. knif, AS. cnif; akin to D. knijf, Icel. knifr, Sw. knif, Dan. kniv.

knight.etymology: OE. knight, cniht, knight, soldier, As. cniht, cneoht, a boy, youth, attendant, military follower; akin to D. & G. knecht servant; perh. akin to E. kin.

knighthood.etymology: Knight + hood: cf. AS. chihthad youth.

knit.etymology: OE. knitten, knutten, As. cnyttan, fr. cnotta knot; akin to Icel. kn, Sw. knyta, Dan. knytte. See Knot.

knob.etymology: A modification of knop. Cf. Nob.

knock.etymology: OE. knoken, AS. cnocian, cnucian; prob. of imitative origin; cf. Sw. knacka.Cf. Knack.

knoll.etymology: AS. cnoll; akin to G. knolle, knollen, clod, lump, knob, bunch, OD. knolle ball, bunch, Sw. knöl, Dan. knold.

knot.etymology: OE. knot, knotte, AS. cnotta; akin to D. knot, OHG. chnodo, chnoto, G. knoten, Icel. kn, Sw. knut, Dan. knude, and perh. to L. nodus. Cf. Knout, Knit.

knout.etymology: Russ. knut'; prob. of Scand. origin; cf. Sw. knut knot, knout, Icel. kn knot: cf. F. knout. See Knot.

know.etymology: OE. knowen, knawen, AS. cnäwan; akin to OHG. chnäan (in comp.), Icel. knä to be able, Russ, znate to know, L. gnoscere, noscere, Gr. jn; fr. the root of E. can, v. i., ken. (Ken, Can to be able, and cf. Acquaint, Cognition, Gnome, Ignore, Noble, Note.

knowledge.etymology: From Middle English knoweleche , knowleche ( “ knowledge ” ) , from late Old English cnāwelǣċ ( “ acknowledgement ” ) , from cnāwan ( “ to know ” ) + -lǣċ(e) , variant of -lāc ( “ -ation ” ) modified after the related verbal suffix -lǣċan . Related to Middle English knowelechen ( “ to find out, acknowledge ” ) , Old English cnāwelǣċing ( “ acknowledging, acknowledgement ” ) .

knuckle.etymology: OE. knokel, knokil, AS. cuncel; akin to D. knokkel, OFries. knokele, knokle, G. knöchel, Sw. knoge, Dan. knokkel, G. knochen bone, and perh. to E. knock.

kraal.etymology: D., a village, inclosure, park, prob. fr. Pg. curral a cattle pen; the same word as Sp. corral. See Corral.

kshatriya.etymology: Skr. kshatriya one belonging to the military caste.

kummel.etymology: G. kümmel cumin, caraway seed, L. cuminum. Cf. Cumin.

roots.meaning: A suffix signifying something written, a writing; also, a writer; as autograph, crystograph, telegraph, photograph.
